extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders, commenters, regulated entities, and legal practitioners participating in or litigating EPA rulemaking under the Clean Air Act (particularly section 202(a))
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive guidance and legal standards for applying the Clean Air Act section 202(a) two-part test (endangerment and cause or contribute) in EPA's Findings on greenhouse gases, and related procedural standards for notice-and-comment rulemaking (comment period adequacy, need for formal rulemaking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of public comment period
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment period must provide a 'meaningful time and a meaningful matter' for participation; EPA found a 120-day period adequate for this action and noted that major scientific assessments relied upon had been previously publicly reviewed and available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting adequacy include length of period (e.g., 120 days), prior public availability and peer review of major technical support documents, multiple submission avenues (docket e-mail, www.regulations.gov, mail, fax), receipt of substantial comments (e.g., voluminous submissions, hundreds of thousands of e-mails), and thorough consideration and response to significant comments in the record. Minor typographical errors in a single notice location do not render the period insufficient if other notice/submission avenues and correct copies existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reopening comment period for alleged missing data
rubrics_metrics.description: A request to reopen or extend the comment period based on alleged unavailability or destruction of original data must show that the absence of those data would materially affect the trends or conclusions relied upon by EPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA will consider whether missing data would materially alter the assessment conclusions. Absent a compelling showing, EPA may rely on multiple independent, peer-reviewed data products (e.g., HadCRUT, NOAA, NASA temperature records), published methodologies for creating quality-controlled/homogenized data, and existing peer-reviewed literature. Release of related synthesis reports that themselves underwent notice-and-comment does not, by itself, require reopening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent proceedings do not automatically require extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The convergence of multiple climate-related proceedings does not by itself render a comment period insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters must show that simultaneous proceedings materially compromised their ability to participate meaningfully. EPA notes it is common for multiple rules to be open at once and will assess whether the public nevertheless had adequate opportunity to comment (e.g., substantial submissions received).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor docket or notice errors do not necessarily deprive due process
rubrics_metrics.description: A typographical error in a notice (e.g., in an e-mail address) does not, standing alone, prevent meaningful public participation or deprive parties of due process if correct information was available elsewhere and multiple submission methods existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether correct information appeared in other authoritative sources (signature version on website, instructions for submitting comments), whether parties were able to submit comments by other means, and whether the docket received broad participation despite the error (e.g., large number of e-mails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal APA on-the-record rulemaking not required without statutory trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking under APA sections 556–557 (i.e., 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing') is only required when a statute explicitly calls for it; the mere mention of the word 'hearing' does not trigger formal APA provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For actions governed by the Clean Air Act, CAA section 307(d) may supply the applicable procedures rather than APA formal rulemaking. Courts recognize formal rulemaking as rarely used; agencies should apply the procedure that the controlling statute requires. Case law: United States v. Florida East Coast Ry. Co., 410 U.S. 224 (1973).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use governing statutory rulemaking procedures (CAA section 307(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the statute (here, the CAA) prescribes specific rulemaking provisions (e.g., CAA section 307(d)), the agency must follow those provisions rather than importing APA formal rulemaking procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must demonstrate satisfaction of the statutory requirements that do apply (e.g., notice, comment, hearings as defined by the CAA), and commenters cannot convert non-binding recommendations (e.g., ACUS factors) into mandatory procedures. Failure to use extraneous procedures not required by statute does not, by itself, constitute abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision to use informal rulemaking is not arbitrary if statute permits it
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing informal (notice-and-comment) rulemaking over formal APA rulemaking is reasonable where the applicable statute does not require formal on-the-record procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not overturn an agency for declining to follow extraneous procedures that are not statutorily required (Vermont Yankee principle). Agencies should ensure the chosen process addresses concerns raised by commenters and satisfies the applicable statutory regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment test is precautionary and preventive in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The endangerment provision permits regulatory action before actual harm occurs; 'endanger' means threatened harm and does not require proof of actual injury or probable harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA interprets this as allowing anticipatory protection: the Administrator should be prepared to act to prevent harm. This interpretation is supported by Ethyl Corp. v. EPA and legislative history emphasizing prevention. The standard contemplates acting on threats, not waiting for realized harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment determination requires weighing likelihood and severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining endangerment involves balancing the likelihood (risk) of harm and the severity (magnitude) of harm; the two are reciprocal elements forming a sliding scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Administrator may find endangerment where harms are severe but unlikely, or where harms are likely though less severe. Catastrophic potential can justify a finding even with low probability. The agency must exercise judgment in weighing these factors and reach a reasoned conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator may act despite scientific uncertainty but must avoid speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because scientific knowledge evolves, the Administrator may make decisions recognizing uncertainties and limitations of available data, but must exercise reasoned decision making and avoid speculative inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency decisions may rest on synthesis reports and peer-reviewed literature. The record should show careful consideration of uncertainties and non-speculative reasoning linking evidence to conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cumulative impacts; 'cause or contribute' has a lower threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing 'cause or contribute', the Administrator should consider the cumulative impact of sources of a pollutant rather than focus solely on a single source; 'contribute' implies a lower threshold than being the sole or major cause and the statute does not modify 'contribute' with 'significant' in section 202(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has discretion to determine whether emissions from a source or class of sources meet the contribution standard; trivial or de minimis contributions may not suffice, but a showing of non-trivial contribution is adequate. This permits regulation of many sectors that each contribute to the aggregate problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of vulnerable subpopulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator must consider risks to all parts of the population, including subpopulations who are at greater risk for reasons such as increased susceptibility to adverse health effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vulnerable subgroups face greater risk, that fact may be taken into account in deciding endangerment. Both likelihood and severity for these subgroups are relevant in the balancing analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of possible future controls is irrelevant to endangerment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether subsequent regulatory control measures would prevent or substantially reduce the danger is not a factor to be considered in making the endangerment or cause-or-contribute determinations under CAA section 202(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress separated the decision whether an air pollutant endangers public health/welfare from the decision of how to regulate. The agency's belief about the ultimate effectiveness of controls is not part of the endangerment inquiry; courts (including the Supreme Court in Massachusetts v. EPA) require the agency to base the endangerment finding on relevant scientific evidence, not speculative projections of control efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory minimum of 'significant risk' required for endangerment
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute does not impose a standalone minimum requirement that there be a 'significant risk of harm' for an endangerment finding; endangerment is assessed by weighing risk and severity rather than hitting a pre-set 'significant' threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Ethyl observed that in its facts there was a significant risk, it did not establish 'significant risk' as a universal floor for all endangerment determinations. The Administrator should evaluate the specific balance of likelihood and severity in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency should not shift burden of proof to opponents of endangerment finding
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should not treat opponents as bearing the burden of proving no endangerment; the statute and precedent do not shift burden to show absence of harm onto challengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision-maker (Administrator) bears the responsibility to weigh the evidence and make a reasoned judgment based on the record. Opponents' generalized calls for additional procedures or proof do not alter this allocation absent statutory text.
